blocks.text: **Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)** is an _acquired, isolated_ thrombocytopenia caused by **immune destruction of platelets**. Autoantibodies coat the patient’s own platelets, and macrophages of the reticulo-endothelial system remove them early from the circulation. **Thrombocytopenia** means a platelet count below **150 × 10^9/L**. ITP is _primary_ when no trigger or underlying disease is found and _secondary_ when it accompanies another condition.

blocks.title: Childhood (acute) versus adult (chronic) ITP
rows: Age 2–6 years; boys and girls equally
Abrupt, often after a viral illness (e.g. varicella, measles)
Insidious; a preceding viral illness is unusual
Usually self-limiting; about 80% remit within 6 months
Fluctuating, relapsing; spontaneous remission is rare
Major haemorrhage only with severe thrombocytopenia

blocks.text: ITP is the **commonest immunological disorder in women of childbearing age**, so it often appears in obstetric and gynaecology vignettes (menorrhagia, pregnancy).

Two names, one disease: Davidson’s calls ITP **idiopathic** thrombocytopenic purpura, while Kumar & Clark and most quick sources call it **immune** thrombocytopenic purpura (or immune thrombocytopenia). Accept either in an exam answer.

ITP is **not a single disease**. Some cases arise on their own (primary ITP), and others reflect wider **immune dysregulation**. Davidson’s stresses that the presentation and the mechanism are the **same whatever the cause**, so the work is in finding the underlying condition. Primary adult ITP affects women about **three times** as often as men.

blocks.title: Conditions linked to secondary ITP
items: **Connective tissue (collagen vascular) disease**, especially **SLE**; it may be present at diagnosis or appear years later
**Antiphospholipid syndrome**
**B-cell malignancy and lymphoproliferative disease**: **CLL**, lymphoma; solid tumours are also reported
**Viral infection**: **HIV**, hepatitis C, HSV; in children a recent varicella or measles infection
**Other autoimmune disease**: thyroid disease, and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (**Evans syndrome**)
**Pregnancy**
**Drugs**: e.g. **alemtuzumab** (used in multiple sclerosis) can provoke autoimmune thyroid disease and ITP

blocks.text: **Evans syndrome** = ITP plus autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. It occurs in about **10%** of ITP patients, so check for haemolysis (and a DAT) when the haemoglobin is also low.

Many drugs (e.g. **quinine, vancomycin, heparin**) cause **drug-associated immune thrombocytopenia**. The first step is to stop the drug, so always take a full drug history before labelling a patient as primary ITP.

sections.title: Pathogenesis: antibody-coated platelets and the spleen

blocks.text: The patient makes **IgG autoantibodies**, most often against the platelet membrane **glycoprotein IIb/IIIa** and sometimes **glycoprotein Ib**. Antibody-coated (“sensitised”) platelets bind **Fc receptors on macrophages**, mainly in the **spleen**, and are destroyed early. The marrow responds by making more platelets, so **megakaryocytes increase**. Pocket Medicine adds a second arm: some autoantibodies also target **megakaryocytes**, which lowers platelet production.
Autoantibodies can be shown in only about **60–70%** of patients. In the rest they are assumed to be present but below the detection limit, which is why a negative antibody test does not exclude ITP.

blocks.title: How each treatment targets the mechanism
rows: Reduce autoantibody production and inhibit macrophage phagocytosis of coated platelets
Blocks (saturates) macrophage Fc receptors, so fewer coated platelets are taken up
Antibody-coated red cells overload macrophage Fc receptors (a “decoy”)
Removes the main site of platelet destruction
Anti-CD20: depletes the B cells that make the antibody
Drive megakaryocytes to make more platelets

blocks.text: An increase in marrow megakaryocytes fits any **consumptive** thrombocytopenia. ITP is the classic _immune_ consumptive cause.

Patients usually **feel well**, without fever, weight loss or other systemic symptoms. Bleeding is **mucocutaneous**: petechiae, purpura, easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding and menorrhagia; haematuria or melena can also occur. Apart from the signs of bleeding, the **examination is normal**. Many adults are diagnosed by chance on a routine blood count, especially when the count is above 50 × 10^9/L.

blocks.title: Platelet count and bleeding risk (×10^9/L)
rows: Often no symptoms; found incidentally. Bleeding mainly with trauma or surgery
Spontaneous bleeding: purpura, oral, nasal, GI or GU bleeding
Rare but serious retinal or intracranial haemorrhage

blocks.title: Platelet-type versus coagulation-type bleeding
items: **Platelet problem** (ITP, platelet dysfunction, von Willebrand disease): petechiae, purpura, oozing from small cuts, epistaxis, menorrhagia, GI bleeding; bleeding starts **immediately** after surgery
**Coagulation factor problem** (e.g. haemophilia): bleeding into **muscles and joints** (haemarthroses), deep haematomas and retroperitoneal bleeding; bleeding after surgery is **delayed**
**Petechiae** are flat, pinpoint, **non-blanching** bleeds into the dermis; **palpable** purpura suggests vasculitis instead

blocks.note: Look at: petechial purpura, with flat, pinpoint, non-blanching spots typical of a low platelet count.

blocks.text: ITP patients often bleed **less than the count suggests**. Some have few symptoms even below 5 × 10^9/L, and the risk of spontaneous bleeding below 20 × 10^9/L is lower in ITP than the count alone would predict.

**Splenomegaly is not a feature of ITP.** A palpable spleen points elsewhere: lymphoproliferative disease, hypersplenism from portal hypertension, myeloproliferative disease or infections such as malaria and visceral leishmaniasis.

ITP is a **diagnosis of exclusion**. It is made from the history, examination, full blood count and **blood film** once other causes of a low platelet count have been ruled out. The low platelet count must be the **only** abnormality on the count. Platelet autoantibody testing is **not needed** for the diagnosis.

blocks.title: Core tests and expected results
items: **FBC**: isolated thrombocytopenia (usually below 100 × 10^9/L); haemoglobin and white cells normal
**Blood film**: the single most useful first test. Normal red and white cells, few platelets (often **large** ones), and **no red cell fragments, blasts or clumps**
**Bone marrow** (only if atypical): **normal or increased megakaryocytes** with normal cellularity. Davidson’s describes an obvious increase
**Coagulation screen** (PT, APTT, fibrinogen): used to exclude DIC, in which platelets and clotting factors are consumed together, so the PT and APTT are prolonged and fibrinogen falls

blocks.title: Search for a secondary cause
rows: A positive result changes treatment; isolated thrombocytopenia may be its first sign
Treating HCV can raise the count; check HBsAg and anti-HBc before rituximab or IVIG
ANA and other autoantibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies
H. pylori test and pregnancy test

blocks.text: **Pseudothrombocytopenia**: a clotted sample or EDTA-induced **platelet clumping** makes the analyser report a falsely low count. Always look at the **film** (or have the count confirmed manually) before diagnosing ITP.

Age cut-off for a marrow: Davidson’s suggests considering it in patients **over 65** to look for B-cell malignancy, while First Aid says **over 60**. Follow Davidson’s. All sources agree that marrow is also needed for atypical features, such as other cytopenias or an abnormal film.

blocks.note: Look at: the stepwise approach to thrombocytopenia, from repeating the count and checking the film to sorting by destruction versus underproduction.

blocks.title: Causes of thrombocytopenia by mechanism
rows: Aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, myeloma, myelofibrosis, myelodysplasia, B12/folate deficiency, cytotoxic drugs, inherited thrombocytopathies
Few megakaryocytes; usually other cell lines affected (blasts, hypersegmented neutrophils, leukoerythroblastic film)
ITP, drugs (quinine, vancomycin, heparin), post-transfusion purpura, neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia
Red cell fragments (schistocytes); DIC has abnormal clotting tests
Gestational thrombocytopenia, type 2B von Willebrand disease
Context: towards the end of pregnancy, resolving after delivery (gestational); von Willebrand studies (type 2B)

blocks.title: Key mimics of ITP
rows: Fever, fluctuating neurology, MAHA with red cell **fragments**, often AKI, very high LDH; coagulation screen normal; low ADAMTS-13; **platelet transfusion contraindicated**; treat with plasma exchange
MAHA + thrombocytopenia + **renal failure**, without the prominent neurology and fever of TTP
Platelets fall by **more than 30%**, typically **5–14 days** after starting heparin; causes **thrombosis**, not bleeding
Sudden severe thrombocytopenia after a red cell transfusion in someone sensitised by earlier transfusion or pregnancy (usually anti-HPA-1a); IVIG if severe
HPA-1a-negative mother makes antibody against the fetus’s HPA-1a-positive platelets; the platelet equivalent of haemolytic disease of the newborn
Commonest cause in pregnancy; mild, late in pregnancy, resolves after delivery, no harm, no treatment

blocks.title: Purpura with a normal platelet count
items: Senile purpura and factitious purpura
Henoch–Schönlein purpura and other **vasculitis** (palpable purpura)
Paraproteinaemias
Purpura fulminans, e.g. DIC with sepsis

blocks.note: Look at panel E: red cell fragments. Fragments plus a low platelet count suggest TTP, HUS or DIC, not ITP.
Look at: the causes of thrombocytopenia grouped as decreased production, increased destruction and redistribution.

blocks.text: HIT timing differs between sources: Davidson’s gives a fall of more than 30% at **5–14 days**, while Pocket Medicine quotes **4–10 days** with a fall of more than 50%. Use Davidson’s figures. Earlier onset is possible after recent heparin exposure.
Thrombocytopenia **plus fragments plus confusion or fever** means TTP until proven otherwise. Do not transfuse platelets; arrange urgent plasma exchange.

Treat the **patient’s bleeding**, not the number. Stable adults with a count **above 30 × 10^9/L** and no bleeding usually need **no treatment**, except to cover high-risk events such as surgery or biopsy. Even lower counts may be watched if there is no spontaneous bruising or bleeding.

blocks.alt: Treatment ladder for adult ITP: observe if stable with platelets above 30; high-dose glucocorticoid for spontaneous bleeding; add IVIG for major mucosal bleeding or slow response, with platelets if life-threatening; second-line therapies after two relapses or refractory disease.

blocks.title: Treatment options in adult ITP
rows: High-dose glucocorticoid: **prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily** or **dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days**
About two-thirds respond, but relapse is common as the dose is reduced; only a minority have a lasting remission
For severe bleeding, major mucosal bleeding or a slow steroid response, and when a **rapid rise** is needed (e.g. before surgery); about 80% respond within 24–48 h, but the effect lasts only weeks
Only if Rh(D)-positive; avoid if there is haemolysis
Second line (after 2 relapses or refractory disease)
Licensed for ITP; about 75% respond, usually within 10–14 days
Complete remission in about 70%, with improvement in a further 20–25%
Can induce remission; not licensed for ITP
For intracranial or other extreme haemorrhage only

blocks.title: Special situations
items: **Children**: usually no treatment because the illness is short-lived; treat only serious bleeding or before urgent surgery. IVIG raises the count faster than steroids alone

**Pregnancy**: glucocorticoids and/or IVIG, aiming for platelets **above 80 × 10^9/L at delivery** in case spinal anaesthesia or caesarean section is needed; the fetus may also become thrombocytopenic
**Secondary ITP**: treat the cause, e.g. treating HCV or HIV can lift the count

**Splenectomy precautions**: pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal C and influenza vaccines **at least 2–3 weeks before** elective surgery; then **lifelong penicillin V** (a macrolide if allergic), pneumococcal boosters at least 5-yearly, and an alert card or bracelet

blocks.text: **Platelet transfusion** is not routine in ITP: the autoantibody destroys transfused platelets as fast as the patient’s own. Keep it for **life-threatening haemorrhage** (e.g. intracranial bleeding), given alongside IVIG and steroids.

Thresholds and order differ between books. Davidson’s, Kumar & Clark Essentials and First Aid use **30 × 10^9/L** as the level above which treatment is not needed, while Pocket Medicine uses **50 × 10^9/L**. Kumar & Clark Essentials makes splenectomy _the_ second-line therapy, while Davidson’s says the best order is unclear and favours the **licensed TPO-receptor agonists**. Follow Davidson’s.

cards.back: An acquired, isolated thrombocytopenia caused by autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets by reticulo-endothelial macrophages.
Children (2–6 y, post-viral): abrupt and usually self-limiting, about 80% remit within 6 months. Adults (mostly women 20–40): insidious and chronic, rarely remits spontaneously.

cards.front: Name four conditions associated with secondary ITP.
cards.back: SLE/connective tissue disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, B-cell malignancy (CLL, lymphoma), HIV (and HCV) infection; also pregnancy and some drugs.
ITP plus autoimmune haemolytic anaemia; seen in about 10% of ITP patients.

cards.front: Main antigen targeted by ITP autoantibodies?
cards.back: Platelet membrane glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (sometimes glycoprotein Ib).

cards.front: How does IVIG raise the platelet count in ITP?
cards.back: It blocks Fc receptors on reticulo-endothelial macrophages, so fewer antibody-coated platelets are phagocytosed.

cards.front: Below which platelet count does spontaneous bleeding usually start?
cards.back: Below 20 × 10^9/L. Retinal or intracranial haemorrhage is a rare risk below 10 × 10^9/L.

cards.front: Patient with suspected ITP has a palpable spleen. Significance?
cards.back: Splenomegaly is rare in ITP; look for another diagnosis (e.g. lymphoproliferative disease, hypersplenism).
Normal apart from markedly reduced (often large) platelets: no fragments, blasts or platelet clumps.

cards.front: When is a bone marrow examination indicated in suspected ITP?
cards.back: Atypical features (other cytopenias, abnormal film, splenomegaly) or older age (Davidson’s: over 65) to look for B-cell malignancy.
A blood film: look for platelet clumps or a clotted sample (EDTA artefact).
TTP: fever, fluctuating neurology, red cell fragments, AKI, very high LDH, low ADAMTS-13. ITP: isolated low platelets with an otherwise normal film.
A platelet fall of more than 30% about 5–14 days after starting heparin, with thrombosis rather than bleeding.

cards.front: Platelet level above which a stable adult with ITP usually needs no treatment?
cards.back: Above 30 × 10^9/L (unless surgery or a biopsy is planned).

cards.front: First-line treatment for ITP with spontaneous bleeding?
cards.back: High-dose glucocorticoid: prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily or dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days (add IVIG for severe bleeding).
TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), splenectomy (about 70% complete remission), and immunosuppression such as rituximab.

cards.front: ITP in pregnancy: platelet target at delivery?
cards.back: Above 80 × 10^9/L, using glucocorticoids and/or IVIG, in case of spinal anaesthesia or caesarean section.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is found to have a platelet count of 22 × 10^9/L. Her haemoglobin, white cell count and film are otherwise normal, and a diagnosis of primary ITP is made.
questions.leadIn: Against which structure are her autoantibodies most likely directed?
questions.explanation: ITP autoantibodies most often target the platelet membrane **glycoprotein IIb/IIIa** (sometimes Ib). Coated platelets are then removed by macrophages.
whyNot: Antibodies to ADAMTS-13 cause acquired TTP.
Antibodies to the PF4–heparin complex cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
Rh(D) antibodies target red cells; anti-D is used as a treatment “decoy”, not the cause.
Von Willebrand factor is not the autoantibody target in ITP.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy develops widespread petechiae and nosebleeds 2 weeks after chickenpox. His platelet count is 15 × 10^9/L with an otherwise normal blood count and film. He is well and has no spleen palpable.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely course of his condition?
options: Lifelong need for a TPO-receptor agonist
questions.explanation: Post-viral childhood ITP is usually **self-limiting**: about 80% resolve spontaneously within 6 months, so most children need no treatment.
whyNot: Chronic ITP is unusual in children; splenectomy is not expected.
An otherwise normal count and film argue against leukaemia.
Late connective tissue disease is described mainly in adult ITP.
Long-term TPO-receptor agonists are for refractory adult disease.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has joint pains, a photosensitive facial rash and mouth ulcers. She now has petechiae on her legs. Platelets are 18 × 10^9/L; haemoglobin and white cells are normal, and there are no red cell fragments.
questions.leadIn: Which underlying condition is most likely?
questions.explanation: Arthralgia, a photosensitive rash and mouth ulcers suggest **SLE**, the classic connective tissue disease associated with secondary ITP.
whyNot: CLL is a recognised cause of secondary ITP, but it would not explain her rash, joint pains and mouth ulcers.
Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
B12 deficiency lowers production and usually affects other cell lines (macrocytosis).
Haemophilia causes joint and muscle bleeding with a normal platelet count.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with known ITP becomes tired and jaundiced. Haemoglobin is 84 g/L, platelets 20 × 10^9/L, and the film shows spherocytes and polychromasia but no fragments. The direct antiglobulin test is positive. Clotting tests are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Immune thrombocytopenia plus **DAT-positive** autoimmune haemolysis (spherocytes) is **Evans syndrome**.
whyNot: TTP causes MAHA with red cell fragments and a negative DAT.
HUS also shows fragments with renal failure; the DAT is negative.
DIC would show abnormal clotting tests.
She is not pregnant, and gestational thrombocytopenia causes no haemolysis.

questions.stem: A patient with ITP and wet purpura is given intravenous immunoglobulin, and the count rises within 2 days.
questions.leadIn: What is the main mechanism of this rise?
questions.explanation: IVIG saturates **Fc receptors** on reticulo-endothelial macrophages, so antibody-coated platelets are not cleared.
whyNot: This is how romiplostim and eltrombopag work.
This is how rituximab works; it is not the mechanism of IVIG.
Plasma exchange replaces ADAMTS-13 in TTP.
SYK inhibition is how fostamatinib works.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with isolated thrombocytopenia has an atypical history, so a bone marrow examination is done. The final diagnosis is ITP.
questions.leadIn: Which marrow finding fits this diagnosis?
options: Sheets of blasts replacing the marrow
questions.explanation: Peripheral destruction drives a compensatory **increase in megakaryocytes**; cellularity is otherwise normal.
whyNot: This suggests aplastic anaemia (reduced production).
Blasts indicate leukaemia.
Megaloblastic change indicates B12 or folate deficiency.
Fibrosis indicates myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is referred with a platelet count of 28 × 10^9/L and bruising. The referral letter queries ITP.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding should most strongly make you doubt that diagnosis?
options: Spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin
A history of heavy menstrual bleeding
Few symptoms despite the low count
questions.explanation: The examination in ITP is **normal apart from bleeding**; **splenomegaly is rare** and should prompt a search for another diagnosis.
whyNot: Petechiae are typical of thrombocytopenia.
Menorrhagia is a common presentation.
Epistaxis is common in ITP.
ITP patients often bleed less than the count suggests.

questions.stem: A medical student asks at what platelet count patients usually begin to bleed spontaneously.
questions.leadIn: Below which count does spontaneous bleeding typically begin?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous bleeding typically appears only **below 20 × 10^9/L**. Higher counts cause bruising or bleeding after trauma.
whyNot: This is the lower limit of normal.
Abnormal bleeding is unusual above 100.
Between 20 and 50, bleeding mainly follows trauma or surgery.
Major bleeding becomes more likely at this level, but spontaneous bleeding starts higher.

questions.stem: A well 46-year-old man has a routine count of 42 × 10^9/L. He has no bruising or bleeding, and his haemoglobin and white cells are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Examine a blood film for platelet clumps
questions.explanation: An unexpected low count in a well patient may be **pseudothrombocytopenia** from clumping or a clotted sample. The **blood film** is the first test.
whyNot: Treatment is not indicated without bleeding, and the count may be spurious.
Marrow is reserved for atypical features.
Transfusion is not indicated for an asymptomatic count.
Antibody testing is not required and would not exclude an artefact.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has isolated thrombocytopenia of 24 × 10^9/L with a normal film apart from few platelets. He has no lymphadenopathy.
questions.leadIn: Davidson’s recommends considering a bone marrow examination at his age mainly to look for which associated condition?
questions.explanation: In patients **over 65**, a marrow is considered to detect an accompanying **B-cell malignancy**, a recognised cause of secondary ITP.
whyNot: Aplastic anaemia usually lowers all cell lines.
Myelofibrosis gives a leukoerythroblastic film and a big spleen.
Megaloblastic anaemia would show macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils.
Gaucher disease causes marrow infiltration with splenomegaly.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought in confused and febrile. Platelets are 12 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 82 g/L with red cell fragments, LDH is very high and creatinine is raised. PT and APTT are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fever, fluctuating neurology, MAHA with **fragments**, AKI and a very high LDH with **normal clotting** is TTP (ADAMTS-13 deficiency).
whyNot: ITP has a normal film apart from few platelets and no organ dysfunction.
Evans syndrome causes spherocytes with a positive DAT, not fragments.
DIC prolongs the PT/APTT.
There is no heparin exposure, and HIT causes thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is on unfractionated heparin after a hip replacement. On day 9 his platelets fall from 280 to 120 × 10^9/L and his calf swells; a DVT is confirmed.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of the low platelets?
questions.explanation: A fall of **more than 30%** about **5–14 days** after starting heparin, with **thrombosis**, is HIT (anti-PF4/heparin antibodies activate platelets).
whyNot: ITP causes bleeding, not thrombosis, and has no link to the heparin timing.
PTP follows a transfusion and causes severe bleeding.
DIC needs a trigger such as sepsis and gives abnormal clotting tests.
Dilution follows massive transfusion.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with known ITP has a platelet count of 45 × 10^9/L. She has no bruising or bleeding and no procedure planned.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Stable patients with counts **above 30 × 10^9/L** and no bleeding usually need **no treatment**.
whyNot: Steroids are for spontaneous bleeding.
IVIG is for severe bleeding or a needed rapid rise.
Transfused platelets are destroyed; they are kept for life-threatening bleeding.
Splenectomy is a second-line option after relapses.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has a splenectomy for refractory ITP.
questions.leadIn: Which long-term measure is recommended afterwards?
questions.explanation: After splenectomy, **lifelong penicillin V** (a macrolide if allergic) is recommended, with pneumococcal boosters at least 5-yearly and an alert card.
whyNot: Aspirin has no role in preventing post-splenectomy sepsis.
Steroids are not needed if the splenectomy works.
IVIG is not a maintenance treatment after splenectomy.
TPO-RAs are an alternative to splenectomy, not routine afterwards.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient described below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has 2 weeks of bruises and heavy periods. Platelets are 14 × 10^9/L; haemoglobin and white cells are normal, and the film shows only reduced platelets. No spleen is palpable.
items.explanation: Isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal film and examination in a young woman is ITP.

items.stem: A healthy 33-year-old woman at 38 weeks of pregnancy has platelets of 108 × 10^9/L at a routine check. Her blood pressure is normal, and her count early in the pregnancy was normal.
items.explanation: A mild fall late in an uncomplicated pregnancy is gestational thrombocytopenia, the commonest cause in pregnancy.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman who has had three pregnancies receives red cells after surgery. A few days later she develops widespread purpura with platelets of 4 × 10^9/L. Anti-HPA-1a antibody is found.
items.explanation: Severe thrombocytopenia after transfusion in a previously sensitised woman with anti-HPA-1a is post-transfusion purpura.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites has platelets of 70 × 10^9/L and white cells of 3.4 × 10^9/L. The spleen is palpable.
items.explanation: Two steps: cirrhosis causes portal hypertension and splenic enlargement, and the big spleen pools platelets (hypersplenism).

questions.theme: Management of ITP and its mimics
questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient described below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Platelet transfusion with IVIG and glucocorticoid
Stop heparin and give an alternative anticoagulant
Antiviral treatment of the underlying infection

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with ITP has an incidental platelet count of 38 × 10^9/L. He has no bleeding, and no surgery is planned.
items.explanation: Above 30 × 10^9/L with no bleeding, no treatment is needed.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman newly diagnosed with ITP has scattered petechiae on her legs and some bruising. There is no mucosal bleeding. Platelets are 9 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: Spontaneous bleeding is the indication for first-line high-dose glucocorticoid.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with ITP and platelets of 3 × 10^9/L develops a sudden severe headache. CT shows an intracranial haemorrhage.
items.explanation: Life-threatening bleeding is the one situation where platelets are transfused, together with IVIG and steroids.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has fever, confusion, platelets of 10 × 10^9/L, red cell fragments and a very high LDH. Clotting tests are normal.
items.explanation: This is TTP: plasma exchange replaces ADAMTS-13 and removes the antibody. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient described below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A well 36-year-old woman has a platelet count of 35 × 10^9/L on a pre-employment check. She has never bruised easily. What is the single most useful first test?
items.explanation: Step 1: an unexpected low count in a well person may be artefact. Step 2: the film shows clumps or a clot (pseudothrombocytopenia) and also screens for fragments or blasts. So the film comes first.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has isolated thrombocytopenia of 20 × 10^9/L. The film is otherwise normal, and there is no other obvious cause. Which test looks for an associated malignancy?
items.explanation: Step 1: ITP in someone this old can be secondary to B-cell malignancy. Step 2: Davidson’s advises considering a marrow examination over age 65. So the answer is bone marrow.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with refractory ITP is about to start rituximab. Which test must be checked first?
items.explanation: Step 1: rituximab depletes B cells and can reactivate hepatitis B. Step 2: so check HBsAg and anti-HBc first, and before IVIG, which can confuse the serology.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with ITP has responded to prednisolone twice but relapsed each time the dose was reduced. She wishes to avoid surgery.
questions.leadIn: Which second-line treatment works by increasing platelet production?
questions.explanation: Step 1: two relapses means second-line therapy. Step 2: most options act on destruction (splenectomy removes the site of clearance; rituximab, mycophenolate and ciclosporin suppress antibody production). Step 3: only the **TPO-receptor agonists** (romiplostim, eltrombopag) drive megakaryocytes to make more platelets. They are licensed for ITP and work in about 75%, usually within 10–14 days.
whyNot: Rituximab depletes B cells and so reduces antibody production.
Splenectomy removes the main site of platelet destruction, and she wants to avoid surgery.
Mycophenolate is an immunosuppressant.
Ciclosporin is an immunosuppressant.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient described below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has recurrent painful swelling of the knee after minor knocks. Platelet count is normal, and APTT is prolonged. His maternal uncle had a similar problem.
items.explanation: Joint bleeding points to a coagulation factor defect. A prolonged APTT and an X-linked family pattern mean haemophilia A.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has raised, palpable purpura on both legs and blood in his urine. His platelet count is normal.
items.explanation: Palpable purpura with a normal count is vasculitis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent nosebleeds and iron deficiency. There are small red spots on her lips and tongue, and the platelet count is normal.
items.explanation: Telangiectasia of the lips and tongue indicates hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with SLE develops petechiae and gum bleeding. Platelets are 11 × 10^9/L; haemoglobin, white cells and clotting tests are normal, and there are no red cell fragments.
items.explanation: Two steps: an isolated low count without fragments or a clotting defect means immune destruction, and SLE is a classic cause of secondary ITP.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has heavy periods and prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. Her platelet count and PT are normal. Her mother bruises easily.
items.explanation: Mucosal bleeding with a normal count and a family history fits von Willebrand disease, the commonest inherited bleeding disorder.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient described below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 5-year-old girl has petechiae 3 weeks after a viral illness. Platelets are 18 × 10^9/L. She has no mucosal bleeding and is otherwise well.
items.explanation: Childhood ITP is usually short-lived, so treatment is kept for serious bleeding or urgent surgery.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic ITP (platelets 25 × 10^9/L) needs an urgent laparotomy in 2 days, and the count must rise fast.
items.explanation: IVIG gives the quickest rise (within 24–48 hours), so it is used before surgery.

items.stem: A 34-year-old Rh(D)-positive woman with ITP needs a rapid platelet rise, but IVIG is unavailable. She has no evidence of haemolysis.
items.explanation: In Rh(D)-positive patients, anti-D immunoglobulin coats red cells, which then saturate macrophage Fc receptors. Avoid it if there is haemolysis.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman has relapsed twice after glucocorticoids. She is keen to avoid an operation and wants a licensed drug that boosts platelet production.
items.explanation: After two relapses, second-line therapy is indicated. TPO-receptor agonists increase production and are licensed for ITP.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient described below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A newborn has widespread petechiae and a platelet count of 15 × 10^9/L. The mother’s own count is normal, and she is HPA-1a negative.
items.explanation: Two steps: a normal maternal count makes maternal ITP unlikely, and an HPA-1a-negative mother making antibody against fetal platelets is NAIT.

items.stem: A woman at 36 weeks of pregnancy has hypertension, raised liver enzymes, haemolysis and a platelet count of 60 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets in late pregnancy is HELLP.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man started quinine for night cramps 8 days ago. He now has purpura and platelets of 6 × 10^9/L, with an otherwise normal count.
items.explanation: Quinine is a classic cause of drug-associated immune thrombocytopenia; stop the drug.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with known ITP becomes jaundiced and anaemic. The film shows spherocytes, and the direct antiglobulin test is positive.
items.explanation: ITP with DAT-positive autoimmune haemolysis is Evans syndrome.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with chronic ITP is 34 weeks pregnant. Her platelet count is 48 × 10^9/L, and she may need spinal anaesthesia.
questions.leadIn: Above what platelet count should treatment aim to keep her at delivery?
questions.explanation: In pregnancy, glucocorticoids and/or IVIG aim for a count **above 80 × 10^9/L** at delivery in case spinal anaesthesia or caesarean section is needed.
whyNot: This is the non-pregnant observation threshold, not the delivery target.
This is the threshold for spontaneous bleeding, too low for neuraxial anaesthesia.
A normal count is not required.
This is the transfusion threshold in marrow failure.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with ITP has relapsed after two courses of steroids. He chooses splenectomy and asks how likely it is to work.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson’s, about what proportion of patients achieve complete remission after splenectomy?
questions.explanation: Splenectomy produces **complete remission in about 70%**, with improvement in a further 20–25% in favourable cases.
whyNot: Far too low.
Too low.
Too low; Kumar & Clark says two-thirds normalise their count.
Complete remission is about 70%; the further 20–25% only improve.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best-fitting option for each patient described below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops bruising and petechiae 2 weeks after chickenpox. The film shows only a low platelet count.
items.explanation: Post-viral childhood ITP: autoantibody-coated platelets are cleared by macrophages.

items.stem: A man who had a road traffic accident received 15 units of red cells and fluid within a few hours. His platelets are now 45 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: Massive transfusion of platelet-poor products dilutes the platelets.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has back pain, a raised calcium, a serum paraprotein and pancytopenia.
items.explanation: Two steps: the paraprotein, hypercalcaemia and bone pain mean myeloma, and the marrow is infiltrated, so production falls.

items.stem: A man with pneumococcal sepsis oozes from his cannula sites. Platelets are 30 × 10^9/L, PT and APTT are prolonged, and fibrinogen is low.
items.explanation: Low platelets with prolonged clotting times and low fibrinogen in sepsis mean DIC: platelets and clotting factors are both consumed.

items.stem: A 50-year-old vegan has macrocytic anaemia, hypersegmented neutrophils and a platelet count of 70 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: B12 deficiency causes ineffective megaloblastic production, usually affecting more than one cell line.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has a week of petechiae, bruising and mild gum bleeding. Platelets are 9 × 10^9/L; the rest of the count and the film are normal. She has no neurological symptoms.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous bleeding in ITP is treated first-line with **high-dose glucocorticoid** (prednisolone 1 mg/kg or dexamethasone 40 mg for 4 days). IVIG is added for severe mucosal bleeding or a slow response.
whyNot: Splenectomy is second-line, after relapses or refractory disease.
TPO-receptor agonists are second-line.
Rituximab is second-line immunosuppression.
She has spontaneous bleeding, so treatment is indicated.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a platelet count of 15 × 10^9/L. Her doctor must decide between ITP and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
questions.leadIn: Which finding best supports TTP rather than ITP?
options: Red cell fragments on the blood film
questions.explanation: Microangiopathic haemolysis with **red cell fragments** (with a high LDH) is the hallmark of TTP. In ITP the film is normal apart from few platelets.
whyNot: Severe thrombocytopenia occurs in both.
Purpura occurs in both.
Clotting tests are normal in both, because TTP does not consume clotting factors.
Sex does not separate them: ITP is typical in young women, and TTP also affects women, with up to a quarter of cases around pregnancy.

ospe.identify: Petechial purpura: flat, pinpoint, non-blanching skin bleeds. This points to thrombocytopenia (such as ITP) or platelet dysfunction; next step is an FBC and film.
Panel E, red cell fragments (schistocytes): intravascular/microangiopathic haemolysis. With low platelets, think TTP, HUS or DIC; fragments are absent in ITP.
Algorithm for a low platelet count: exclude pseudothrombocytopenia on the film, then decide between destruction (large platelets, fragments) and underproduction (other cytopenias, blasts).
Causes of thrombocytopenia sorted into decreased production, increased destruction (immune and non-immune) and redistribution (splenic sequestration).
